02 · Honest Update

The mark on my wrist
— what actually caused it

THENIrritation visible
NOWCurrent status
  • Not an infection — it's a classic moisture + friction irritation pattern from near-continuous wear, not the ring-shaped scaly look you'd see with a fungal reaction
  • What fixed it: stopped wearing the band on that wrist, kept the area clean and fully dry, avoided scratching, used a plain fragrance-free moisturizer
  • Before restarting: cleaned the strap underside thoroughly, wore it looser, and now remove it for a few hours daily
When to actually worry: if it turns very itchy, spreads, develops bumps or pus, feels warm or painful, or doesn't improve within 5–7 days of resting the wrist — get it examined. Don't self-treat with a random antifungal or steroid cream just because it's red.

References: own photos, 10-day wear period, Aug 2026 · general dermatology guidance on friction/occlusion-related skin irritation — not a medical diagnosis

03 · Straps

Two straps isn't a bonus
— it's the system

Treating the second strap as a "free extra" was my mistake — here's why rotating both actually matters, especially after topic 2.

Strap A — daily wear

Use for regular hours and sleep tracking. Gets the most skin contact time, so it needs regular cleaning.

Strap B — gym / sweat sessions

Swap in before workouts. Keeps sweat exposure off your daily strap and gives strap A time to fully dry.

Why it matters: rotating straps is what actually prevents the skin issue from topic 2 — this isn't optional if you sweat regularly.
